findings.title: Missing Prisma import breaks the app-store build
findings.body: This new call references `prisma`, but this module does not import or otherwise define it. TypeScript cannot resolve the name, so the app-store build/type-check fails. Import the Prisma client before using it here.

findings.title: The sync path returns a Fetch Response to callers expecting token objects
findings.body: When credential syncing is enabled, this returns the raw Fetch `Response`, unlike the provider-specific object returned by the normal refresh function. Several callers treat the result as parsed token data: Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads token fields such as `accessToken`, and Bigin/Zoho CRM read `tokenInfo.data`. Those properties are absent on a Fetch `Response`, so refreshes fail or persist unusable credentials. Parse the response and adapt it to each caller's expected token shape.

findings.title: The minimum schema strips the expiry and refresh-token fields
findings.body: These computed property names are literal strings, not a wildcard for arbitrary token fields, and `z.object` strips unrecognized response properties. Thus a sync response containing `access_token` and `expiry_date` is parsed down to `access_token`; the parser then adds the literal placeholder `refresh_token`. Zoom subsequently uses the missing `expires_in` to compute a NaN expiry and persists the placeholder refresh token, leaving the credential unusable. Preserve and validate the actual expiry field and retain the existing refresh token when the sync response omits one.

findings.title: Webex rejects the documented minimal sync response
findings.body: The sync endpoint is documented in `refreshOAuthTokens` as returning only an access token and expiry, but Webex still validates the parsed response against `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A response following the documented sync contract therefore fails validation and no refreshed token is saved. Handle the minimal response while retaining the old refresh-token metadata, or define a compatible endpoint contract.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint
findings.body: This new refresh path calls Salesforce directly and never uses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so configuring `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no effect for Salesforce. Salesforce credentials therefore continue to refresh locally instead of using the external app store as the source of truth, leaving this integration outside the feature.

findings.title: Bigin sends the credential ID as the Cal.com user ID
findings.body: The third argument is serialized by `refreshOAuthTokens` as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the credential row's ID rather than the user's ID. The sync endpoint will look up the wrong user and cannot return that user's Bigin tokens. Pass `credential.userId` instead.

findings.title: Zoom sends an integration name instead of the app slug
findings.body: This argument becomes the sync request's `appSlug`, but Zoom credentials use app ID/slug `zoom` (the OAuth callback creates them with `appId: "zoom"`); `zoomvideo` is the integration type/name. An endpoint that looks up the app by slug will not find Zoom and cannot return the user's tokens. Pass `zoom` here.

findings.title: Replacing a credential does not clear its invalid state
findings.body: When an existing credential has been marked invalid, this update replaces only its key and leaves `invalid` set. The app will continue to treat the newly synced credentials as invalid, so this endpoint cannot recover a connection after the parent platform supplies valid replacement credentials. Clear the invalid flag when accepting a replacement key.
